newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan recovery gradually strengthening--BOJ chief.
newsitem.headline: Japan recovery gradually strengthening--BOJ chief.

text.p: Japan's economy is continuing its gradual recovery and the strength of the recovery is gradually increasing, Bank of Japan (BOJ) Governor Yasuo Matsushita said on Monday.
Matsushita, speaking to a meeting of BOJ branch managers, also said that the central bank was keeping close watch on the impact on the economy of falls in Japanese share prices.
He said BOJ monetary policy would continue to emphasise securing economic recovery, but that private-sector demand needed to strengthen in order for the recovery to be sustained.
"Our economy is continuing its gradual recovery, and the strength of economic recovery is starting to gain in firmness," Matsushita said.
"It is necessary to carefully verify the reason for the recent stock price fall and its impact on the economy," he said.
Concerning the BOJ's current monetary policy, he said, "We think it is appropriate to continue careful watch over developments and put emphasis on securing the basis for economic recovery."

He added that it was important for the economic cycle, centring on private demand, to speed up further in order for the economy to securely move on to a self-sustainable recovery track. Pressures from structural adjustment remained, and support for the economy from fiscal policy was likely to decline, he said.
Matsushita gave a number of reasons for his view that the economy was recovering and that the recovery was gradually gaining in strength.
He said public spending was starting to decline and a decrease in net exports had come to a halt.

Housing investment was at high levels, and private consumption was gradually recovering. Corporate capital spending was steadily rising, and this trend was spreading from large firms to medium-sized and smaller firms, he said.
The tempo of increase in production was speeding up after recovering in the latter half of 1996, helped by growing demand and inventory adjustments.
Prices had also generally stopped falling, he said.
